# Files

Reading and writing files is the heart of day 1: the practical asks you to walk
a directory of alignment reports, parse each one, and write a summary table.
Everything you need is in this chapter.

## Opening and closing a file

```python
fd = open("file_name", "opening mode")
```

The first argument is the path, the second is the mode:

| Mode | Meaning |
|:---:|:---|
| `"r"` | read |
| `"w"` | write, **overwriting** the file if it exists |
| `"a"` | write, appending to the end if it exists |
| `"x"` | write, failing if the file already exists |

Python treats files as text (UTF-8) by default.

```{python}
fd = open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r")
fd
```

::: {.callout-note}
The path is relative to the folder you run the program from, and `/` works on
Linux, macOS and Windows alike. Write it as a plain string:
`"data/fichier_tabulate.tsv"`.
:::

`fd` is an object representing the open file. Once you are done with it, you
must close it:

```{python}
fd.close()
fd
```

## The with statement

Opening a file with [with]{.keywords} is strongly advised: it closes the file
for you, even if an error occurs inside the block. Instead of

```python
fd = open("file.txt", "r")
print(fd.read())
fd.close()
```

write

```python
with open("file.txt", "r") as fd:
    print(fd.read())
```

![The `with` statement opens the file, hands it to you as `fd`, and closes it
on its own when the block ends.](../img/files.png)

::: {.callout-important}
The file is open **only inside** the [with]{.keywords} block.
:::

Two files can be opened at once — a pattern you will use to read a file and
write its transformed version:

```python
with open("filename_in.txt", "r") as in_file, open("filename_out.txt", "w") as out_file:
    in_file.read()
    out_file.write("text")
```

## Reading

A file has a **cursor** that advances as you read. `read()` consumes the whole
file; reading again returns an empty string until you rewind with `seek(0)`.

```{python}
with open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r") as fd:
    whole_file = fd.read()       # everything, as one string
    second_attempt = fd.read()   # the cursor is at the end: empty
    fd.seek(0)                   # rewind
    after_rewind = fd.read()

print("whole file     :", repr(whole_file))
print("second attempt :", repr(second_attempt))
print("after rewind   :", repr(after_rewind))
```

`read(n)` reads *n* characters, `readline()` one line, `readlines()` every line
as a list:

```{python}
with open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r") as fd:
    print("read(3)    :", repr(fd.read(3)))

with open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r") as fd:
    print("readline() :", repr(fd.readline()))

with open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r") as fd:
    print("readlines():", fd.readlines())
```

The idiomatic way is to loop directly over the file, which reads one line at a
time and never loads the whole file into memory:

```{python}
with open("data/fichier_tabulate.tsv", "r") as fd:
    for line in fd:
        print(repr(line))
```

:::{.callout-warning}
Lines read by [readline]{.keywords}, [readlines]{.keywords} and the `for` loop
keep their line break (`\n`). Call `line.strip()` before using them — this is
the single most common source of bugs when parsing files.
:::

## Writing

`write` takes a string, `writelines` a list of strings. Neither adds line
breaks for you.

```{python}
lines_to_write = ['first line', 'second line']

with open("output_file_1.txt", "w") as fout:
    fout.writelines(lines_to_write)

with open("output_file_2.txt", "w") as fout:
    for line in lines_to_write:
        fout.write(line)
```

Open both files in a text editor. What do you see? Can you modify the code so
that each entry really is on its own line?

## Errors and exception handling

When something goes wrong, Python raises an **exception**. Left unhandled, the
program stops and prints the error with its full stack trace. `try` / `except`
lets you catch it and decide what to do.

```{python}
fnamein = "i_dont_exist.svg"

try:
    with open(fnamein, "rb") as fin:
        a = int(fin.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print(f"File {fnamein} does not exist")
except ValueError:
    print("Could not convert the content to an integer")
except OSError as err:
    print("OS error:", err)
```

Catch the **specific** exceptions you expect, from the most precise to the most
general — see the
[hierarchy of exceptions](https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html).

::: {.callout-tip}
In the day 1 practical, one sample has no reads at all and its percentages are
written `N/A`. `float("N/A")` raises a `ValueError`. Deciding what to do with
it is part of the exercise.
:::

Write **exo_file_tsv.py** that reads `data/fichier_tabulate.tsv` and writes an
output file with one extra `sum` column, holding the sum of the other columns
for each row.
